text: A ransomware infection on a single laptop and a multi-week breach of a customer database are both security incidents, but they don't belong in front of the same audience. The concept that sorts them is materiality — whether a reasonable investor would consider the information important to the total mix of information available. That's a legal judgment, never made by the security team alone, and never based on technical severity by itself.

A GRC program that works well has its escalation chain defined before an incident ever happens. The incident response team detects and classifies severity. The CISO is notified immediately above a defined threshold. Legal and privacy counsel assess materiality — this is the exact point where a technical incident becomes a legal and disclosure question. A disclosure committee makes the formal call, and the board or audit committee is briefed from there.

For U.S. public companies, the SEC's 2023 cybersecurity disclosure rules create two real obligations. Form 8-K, Item 1.05 requires disclosing a material incident within four business days — measured from the materiality determination, not from discovery. Form 10-K's Item 106 requires an annual description of how the company manages cyber risk and how the board oversees it. Misreading when that four-day clock actually starts is the most common mistake.

SEC disclosure isn't the only obligation, and it's a mistake to treat it as the whole picture. All fifty states have their own breach notification laws, triggered by exposure of personal data rather than materiality. Sector rules like HIPAA layer on top for healthcare. GDPR requires notifying a supervisory authority within seventy-two hours for organizations subject to EU law — a completely different clock.

The distinction worth keeping: breach notification laws protect individuals and trigger on data exposure, while SEC disclosure protects investors and triggers on materiality to the business. The same incident can trigger both, on different clocks, which is exactly why legal counsel, not the security team, owns deciding which obligations apply. That closes this chapter — the capstone ahead brings the whole path together.
